hansard.speaker: Baroness Kidron (CB)
hansard.text: My Lords, I will speak to my Amendments 172, 278 and 279Q and thank the noble Lords, Lord Tarassenko, Lord Stevenson and Lord Hunt, and the noble Baroness, Lady Finlay, for their support. I also put on the record my support for all the amendments in the name of the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko, to which I added my name. Amendment 172 calls for all NHS patient and public health data to be listed as a sovereign data asset. It builds on the arguments made on 11 November and on Amendment 143 from the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko, but its primary focus is on retaining in the UK the value and the benefits of technology built from NHS data. I too was excited to hear the announcement earlier this week that the University of Warwick and Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust are conducting a trial of AI for the early detection of breast cancer called EDITH. Indeed, I looked to see whether they needed volunteers. But I was disappointed to see on the website that both the secure cloud provider and the chosen software suppliers were US-owned, and that the list of third parties with whom data might be shared included “AI providers”. That is insufficient transparency for data of this value and sensitivity. Even when research is undertaken here in the UK, we need to understand where the economic and technological benefits of that research will ultimately accrue. There is a big difference between feeling that you are contributing to the future of the NHS and making UK health outcomes more dependent on Silicon Valley. This is an argument not against international collaboration but about the terms on which we collaborate. hansard.speaker: Lord Clement-Jones (LD)
hansard.text: My Lords, the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko, and the noble Baroness, Lady Kidron, have made a brilliant case for their amendments. Indeed, one of the most consequential questions in this Bill is how we unlock artificial intelligence and health data for life sciences and public benefit while fiercely protecting patient confidentiality, data sovereignty and public trust. The debates in the Commons over the past week on the NHS federated data platform have brought data sovereignty, supplier lock-in and public trust into sharp relief. Amendment 143 in the name of the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko, and Amendment 172 in the name of the noble Baroness, Lady Kidron, would establish NHS and single patient record data as a sovereign data asset. That means UK-only storage, no routine overseas support access, encryption keys held by NHS bodies and not by suppliers, national security checks on supplier ownership and governance with advice from the National Cyber Security Centre, and reporting to Parliament. The reason is simple. Where data sits in the UK but the supplier is subject to foreign law—the US CLOUD Act is the obvious example—it can be compelled to hand over data held anywhere in the world. Storage location alone is not sovereignty; only control of the keys, of support access and of the software stack protects NHS data from foreign legal compulsion. We all want the UK to lead in health tech and AI-driven drug discovery, but public confidence will evaporate if patients believe their medical histories are being opened up to commercial entities without transparent consent and robust oversight. hansard.speaker: Earl Howe (Con)
hansard.text: My Lords, this has been a thoughtful and wide-ranging debate, and I am grateful to all noble Lords who have tabled and spoken to the amendments in it. This discussion has raised important questions about how we will use new technology in the NHS and how we make the most of the extraordinary resource that NHS data represents. That question has two sides. The first is opportunity. We would be foolish not to see AI as something we can increasingly use to improve productivity and as something that could save money while improving care. Indeed, the Government are relying on it. The NHS settlement in the spending review assumes productivity growth of 2% a year; historically, the health service has averaged nearer 0.6%. The 10-year health plan speaks of making the NHS “the most AI-enabled care system in the world”. These are substantial aspirations. The second side follows from the first, and the noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko, brought it home to us vividly. When the reliance on this technology is so great, it impresses upon us that it must be done responsibly and carefully. Patient safety and the protection of information must be at its heart, and it must be done in a way that allows this country to remain self-reliant and secure. Those are precisely the concerns that noble Lords have raised. On research, Amendments 142 and 278 complement each other. The first concerns the legal gateway through which confidential patient information may be used for research in the public interest. The second concerns the practical service through which researchers would obtain usable data. Anyone who has spoken to researchers will know the frustration of fragmented datasets, inconsistent approvals and months lost to cleaning up data. But public trust is the licence on which all of this depends.

hansard.speaker: Lord Patel (CB)

I support all the amendments that are asking for sovereign data assets and sovereign data platforms. How are we going to curate, own and use it for our own purposes in all the public sector, including the NHS? The UK needs a compute strategy pretty soon.

In my Amendment 172A, I am asking for a clear, consistent rule on when a patient's data has been properly anonymised: that is, when people cannot be identified in any way. That falls outside the scope of data protection law. Pseudonymisation is when the data cannot be attributed to a particular subject using technical or organisational methods. It is sometimes termed de-identified data, and it is sometimes confused with encryption. It is subject to data protection law. Pseudonymised data is not simply data with names removed, nor is it always personal data. The problem is that the exact criteria as to how it is defined in law vary across the UK. The anonymisation and pseudonymisation of patient data ensure that information is protected. Published guidance is needed to ensure that all health services have an equal understanding of how to operate within these frameworks in the four nations. Guidance must use identical definitions, based on real-world data environments, with consistent application. Such guidance must also protect data when used across international research groups because patients may be in clinical trials that are being led even from beyond our shores. hansard.text: My Lords, my Amendment 244 is a simple one—albeit again rather bizarrely grouped—so I do not need to detain the Committee for too long. It concerns the interoperability of NHS digital systems across the four nations of the UK. My principal concern is of course for patients in Wales, but I also have sympathy for patients in Scotland, who do not have access to an NHS app at all, and those in Northern Ireland, who have a very limited patient portal called My Care. At present, the NHS app in England and the digital services available to patients in Wales do not provide a seamless, integrated experience. Patients may find that information about appointments, test results, prescriptions or aspects of their medical history are not readily accessible across the border. We all know that illness does not respect borders and neither should access to a patient's medical information. Patients in Wales frequently cross the border into England to access specialist services, hospital treatment and diagnostic facilities. For these patients, the ability of NHS systems to communicate with one another is not a technical luxury; it is fundamental to safe, timely and effective care. The consequences can, of course, be serious. Patients may have to repeat their medical histories, investigations may be duplicated and clinicians may make decisions without having the complete information they need. Many may miss appointments that have been logged on to the wrong app. These avoidable costs to an NHS already under significant pressure are very real. Evidence presented to the Welsh Parliament's Health and Social Care Committee highlighted the real-world difficulties caused by incompatible systems, including a reported case in which a Welsh patient encountered problems with their waiting list status

hansard.speaker: Baroness Merron (Lab)
hansard.text: —what the noble Baroness, Lady Finlay, said, of personal data. The guidance applies to the use of health data and should be considered by organisations across the health service. We do not want to cut across the work in this area; it is already well advanced. I expect that the points raised by my noble friend Lord Mann will be considered by the UISPC, on which there will also be consultation in 2027. The SPR is not intended to be a primary vehicle for recording ethnicity information, because it will draw from existing source systems. It is these systems that will record the appropriate data on protected characteristics that will enable us to monitor and tackle inequalities in health. hansard.speaker: Mr Francois

hansard.debate: Draft AWE Pension Scheme  (Transfer of Assets) Regulations 2026
hansard.speaker: Mary Creagh
hansard.text: Allow me to reminisce if I may, Mr Efford. There is a political point at the end of this. Clearly, the outsourcing moment breaks that link between the beneficiaries and the administrators. In the case of Capita, that is a matter of regret, but we must do the best with what we have. hansard.speaker: Mary Creagh
hansard.text: Not just a pretty face— [ Interruption. ] Speak for yourself, Mark. Have they had the McCloud adjustments applied, and are they included in this transfer? hansard.speaker: Baroness Merron (Lab)
hansard.text: I can give the assurance that all the usual safeguards apply. The EDITH trial is supporting mammogram interpretation and comparing standard double-reading with two assisted pathways. One pathway is using AI after an NHS expert—a human being—has been involved. Another is using AI first, to inform the review by one or two experts: in other words, one or two human beings. AI will not be working alone; it will be working with experts. I hope that is reassuring.

hansard.speaker: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Department of Health and Social Care (Baroness Merron) (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, in the world's largest trial, the NIHR-funded early detection using information technology and health—otherwise known as EDITH—trial will test whether AI can safely help NHS experts detect breast cancer earlier. It will assess whether AI could free up specialist time, enable more women to be screened and perform effectively across different groups of women. Its findings will provide vital evidence to inform decisions about the future use of AI in NHS breast screening.

hansard.speaker: Lord Tarassenko (CB)
hansard.text: My Lords, I declare an interest as senior adviser to the Alan Turing Institute and as the holder of an honorary researcher contract with my local NHS trust. I welcome the fact that the EDITH trial is starting to recruit patients this week. It will help to answer some fundamental questions about the use of AI in radiology: for example, what happens when the AI disagrees with the radiologist when it is one of the two readers of the image? Will the second radiologist, brought in to arbitrate, be told what the decisions of the AI and the first radiologist were? So I ask the Minister: will the full trial protocol be published by the NIHR, the funders, or the co-investigators in an academic journal?

hansard.speaker: Baroness Merron (Lab)
hansard.text: Just last month, we accepted all 44 recommendations from the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare. That will bring clearer regulatory responsibilities to light, and also transparency, and, as the noble Baroness rightly seeks, it will create the right environment for AI research to move safely and efficiently from evaluation into NHS use. So I take the point and feel that we are absolutely moving in that way.

hansard.speaker: Baroness Nargund (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, I thank the Minister for her reply. I congratulate our Government on their investment in this landmark, multicentre breast-screening trial: the world's largest. It has huge potential to improve early breast cancer detection and will have a significant positive impact on women's health. Given that breast cancer rates are rising among young women, and they tend to be more aggressive types that are diagnosed late, leading to poorer outcomes, I ask the Minister what consideration has been given to including younger women in the trial. Also, given the existing health inequalities and potential risk of AI bias, can the Minister assure the House that women from low socioeconomic regions, as well as from ethnic-minority backgrounds, are sufficiently included, and that the sub-group outcomes will be published to ensure that AI-assisted innovation is not only safe but equitable?

hansard.speaker: Baroness Wolf of Dulwich (CB)
hansard.text: My Lords, as recruiters of international students, universities use rather different English language tests from the Home Office. We do online interviews of marginal students to see if they can cope with the course. One can see how instant translation software is being used by more and more people as they are interviewed and talking to us. Many noble Lords will have noted the recent meltdown in the university entrance examinations in Korea because of AI-enabled cheating. Can the Minister tell me how the Government intend to monitor these ongoing threats to online testing in the years ahead?

hansard.speaker: Baroness Nargund
hansard.text: To ask His Majesty's Government what assessment they have made of the potential impact on improving women's health outcomes of the national EDITH trial to use AI to help detect breast cancers earlier.

hansard.speaker: Lord Collins of Highbury (Lab)
hansard.text: The noble Baroness has answered the question. This runs through every part of life. hansard.speaker: Baroness Finlay of Llandaff (CB)

That all sounded great, yet in the same month the Medical Schools Council census revealed a stark and accelerating decline in the number of clinical medical academics, the very doctors who lead research, translate discovery into patient benefit and educate future doctors. Without a strong clinical medical academic workforce, the foundations of both flagship strategies risk being aspirational rather than operational. The Medical Schools Council 2024 census recorded just 3,090 full-time equivalent medical academics in the UK, only 3.4% of consultants, down from 4.7% in 2009. Alarmingly, a third of them are now over 55. Of the professors—the most senior of the medical academics—nearly two-thirds are nearing retirement. The early career roles are vanishing. Those under the age of 36 have dropped by 29% in the last 11 years. Medical academics bridge between science and clinical practice; they are part researcher, part educator and part clinician. hansard.text: I certainly can assure my noble friend that the EDITH trial will run, first of all, within the existing screening programme, and will assess whether AI performs equally across age, ethnicity and socioeconomic groups. On the point about younger women, as my noble friend will be aware, routine screening does begin at 50, which is the independent recommendation by the National Screening Committee. That is because mammograms are less reliable in younger women, due to denser breast tissue. However, I should say that women who are at very high risk can be offered earlier checks. Also, the AgeX trial is currently examining the benefits of screening at a younger age and will report in a few years' time.

hansard.text: I have asked the First Secretary of State to oversee this from her position at the very top of Government, so she will do exactly the job that the right hon. Gentleman asks for. hansard.speaker: Stuart Anderson (South Shropshire) (Con)

As we have heard, in 1982 the nationalist Argentinian Government sought to restore their public approval by making a reckless claim on the Falkland Islands. The Falkland Islanders see themselves as British, and they want to remain British. In 2013, they voted overwhelmingly to remain British. Let me be clear: the Falkland Islands are British. I grew up in Hereford, and my dad, like everybody's in my class, was in the Special Air Service. This debate concerns the greatest single loss of life in the Falkland Islands war: the sinking of the Sir Galahad on 8 June 1982, when 48 brave men died on board after a bombing raid by the Argentinian air force. Thirty-two of those men were brave Welsh Guards. I am clear that those men are heroes, sent to protect the sovereign wishes of Falklanders. They answered the call when it was given. On behalf of His Majesty's Opposition, I thank and honour all those men who answered the call, as well as the women who provided support or served in the Falklands. hansard.text: It is such an important question, resilience. I will address the Liaison Committee on Monday on this very issue. What I can point my hon. hansard.debate: International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women
hansard.speaker: Llinos Medi (Ynys Môn) (PC)
hansard.text: Misogyny on social media normalises violence against women and girls in our communities. This is a direct threat to the safety of women and girls, and as a mum and an auntie to young girls, I refuse to allow it to impact their futures. Does the Minister agree that all of us across the House have a role to play in challenging misogyny at source and preventing real-life consequences? And that means all of us!

hansard.speaker: Mrs Badenoch
hansard.text: The Prime Minister is coming unstuck because he spent more time on vibes than on the detail, so let us see where his vibes get us. He mentioned lockdown parties earlier in his statement, and I think he is going to fall off his high horse very quickly. This week, we saw videos of the Prime Minister hosting social media influencers in Downing Street. The words used by one of them on the steps of No. 10 were so offensive that I will not repeat them in this House: disgusting and pejorative comments about women's private parts, and obscene language that referred to white women as “cheap meat”. This is grotesque. Labour MPs constantly tell us about their commitments to fighting violence against women and girls. Those MPs were silent yesterday; I won't be! Will the Prime Minister now apologise for debasing his office and for allowing that vile video to be recorded on the steps of No. 10?

hansard.debate: International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women
hansard.speaker: The Minister for Women and Equalities (Bridget Phillipson)
hansard.text: These last few weeks have seen our national conversation dominated by accounts of, and finally some accountability for, some of the most grotesque and horrific abuses of male power, not merely to limit the lives of women but, through coercion, control and violence, to seek to scar them and to wreck them. I pay tribute to those survivors who came forward, often in great fear and despite immense pressure. They spoke to the police and spoke in public, and their bravery and moral purpose is a beacon to us all. The stories of what was done to women and what men have got away with have dominated our media and our discussions in a way that is rare, important and incredibly powerful. As we mark the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women, I am proud that, working with ministerial colleagues right across Government, we are bringing action to go further and faster to bring change in our country. I am sure I speak for women everywhere when I say that we have had enough of hoping that reflections on stories like those we have heard again in recent weeks will alone prompt the wider cultural and social change we so desperately need to protect women. There has been much welcome change, but we know that there has not been enough, and we have to meet the moment. We must step up the pace of change to build the country that we all deserve, and that change must come in every corner of our country and in every part of our society. It must also come from this House, through the law and through the courts and the police. Nearly a year ago, we launched our landmark cross-Government strategy to tackle violence against women and girls and to provide freedom from violence and abuse. I pay tribute to amazing colleagues across these Benches who crafted it, steered it and fou

hansard.debate: Code of Practice for Public Authorities Sharing Information with Digital Verification Services
hansard.speaker: Lord Clement-Jones (LD)
hansard.text: My Lords, I thank the Minister for introducing this draft code so comprehensively. From these Benches, we do not oppose the code, but a first statutory code under a new information-sharing power deserves more than a nod through, and I want to set out both what it gets right and where, in our view, it falls short. This is the code for what we called during the passage of the Bill, now the Act, the information gateway. Section 45 lets public authorities disclose what they hold about us to registered digital verification services. As the Minister described, these are passport records, driving licence records and civil registration records held by the Passport Office, the DVLA and the General Register Office. It is the most authoritative data the state holds about any of us. The context has changed since we debated Part 2. In July, the new Prime Minister abandoned the national digital ID scheme announced in September 2025. On these Benches, we opposed mandatory state-issued ID, and we welcomed that decision, but it means that this gateway and the market of certified private providers it feeds is now, in practice, the main route by which people will prove who they are online. That raises the stakes for getting this code right. During the passage of the Bill, I said that high levels of trust in this sector depend on a high level of assurance. I argued that the Bill lacked governance, accountability and effective independent regulation. I said that there was no mechanism for monitoring compliance, investigating malicious actors or taking enforcement action. I tabled amendments on independent oversight, reporting the volume of disclosures to the Information Commissioner, an annual review of this very code, a right to non-digital verification and digital identity theft. hansard.speaker: Lord Patel (CB)
hansard.text: My Lords, before I refer to my own amendment, I say that I support the amendments from the noble Baronesses, Lady Harding and Lady Barker, for the very reasons that they mentioned. In my clinical practice, I was asked many times to keep information that I was given by mothers about their previous reproductive history confidential. That sometimes created a problem in managing their pregnancies, but we had to devise a way of coping with it. These are important issues to be considered for the single patient record. I too support strongly the development of longitudinal patient data in a single patient record, but I have serious concerns about Clause 52(2), which introduces new Section 250E(3). It says: “The regulations may provide that the processing of information in accordance with the regulations does not breach any obligation of confidence”— that is what we are talking about, the confidence and trust that patients can have— “owed by the person processing the information”. hansard.speaker: The Minister for the Armed Forces (Louise Sandher-Jones)
hansard.text: It is a pleasure to serve under your chairship, Sir Jeremy. I give my huge thanks to my hon. Friend the Member for Newport East (Jessica Morden) for securing this incredibly important debate, and I thank each and every Member who has contributed. This is an issue that my hon. Friend has been campaigning on, along with many others, for a long time. I met her and my hon. Friends the Members for Cardiff South and Penarth (Stephen Doughty) and for Neath and Swansea East (Carolyn Harris) in February. I welcome the opportunity to have this conversation and discuss this incredibly important issue. The story begins with the loss of RFA Sir Galahad and the death of 48 people, including 32 members of the Welsh Guards. Many carry the physical and psychological consequences of that tragedy today, and many families have been forced to live their lives without their loved ones. They were in the Falklands fighting to protect British citizens and British territory. I am proud of this country for standing up to recognise the right of the people of the Falkland Islands to self-determination. They have shown time and again that they wish to be British, and I am proud that we defend that. In a world in which large neighbours increasingly feel that they can bite chunks off small neighbours, that principle is absolutely worth defending. hansard.speaker: Baroness Shawcross-Wolfson (Con)
hansard.text: My Lords, nobody in this House doubts the importance of an effective single patient record. Indeed, the NHS has been working towards this idea for decades because, while the idea is simple in theory, the implementation is incredibly difficult. Of course, there is the technical challenge, but as my noble friend Lady Harding reminded us, building trust is even harder. We have seen that from the care.data and GDPR attempts, which failed because patients and clinicians lost confidence in how their data would be used. I thank the Minister and the department for the extensive engagement that they offered us. As she candidly acknowledged in our previous debate, some of the questions asked do not have immediate answers. Indeed, there is a lot that we do not yet know and almost everything that we know comes from departmental assurances, not from Clause 52 itself. First, what is this? The department tells us that it will be a new clinical interface. Does that mean that it is view-only? If so, will that always be the case? Nothing in the Bill says so or would prevent the development of a different model later on. Secondly, how will privacy be protected? The letter from the Minister offers welcome assurances: role-based access, a detailed audit trail and clinicians able, we envisage, to restrict sensitive information. Yet this is only emerging thinking and none of it is in the Bill. Thirdly, who is liable when something goes wrong? We know that NHS organisations remain responsible for their source data, but if information in the SPR is displayed wrongly and a clinician acts on that inaccurate information, who is liable? hansard.speaker: Baroness Sugg (Con)
hansard.text: My Lords, I will speak to Amendment 148 in the name of the noble Baroness, Lady Barker, to which I have added my name, and to other amendments in the group. As we heard from the noble Baroness, Lady Freeman, in her opening remarks on the group, and just now from my noble friend Lady Harding, the success of the single patient record will ultimately depend on trust. If patients trust the system, they will engage with it. If they do not, they may wish to withhold information from clinicians or, indeed, avoid seeking care altogether. That would undermine the very objectives that this reform is intended to achieve. Amendment 148 addresses one of the areas where trust is most fragile: sexual and reproductive healthcare. As I said at Second Reading, I am broadly very supportive of the SPR and recognise the significant benefits that better information sharing can bring, but my concern is that sexual and reproductive health information has always, rightly, been treated differently, as it is uniquely sensitive because disclosure can, in some circumstances, expose patients to real harm. That is particularly true for patients experiencing domestic abuse, coercive control or honour-based abuse. It may also affect young people seeking confidential advice and treatment. I welcome the Government's recognition that some health information requires particular protection, and the assurance that there is no intention simply to make highly sensitive information widely available. However, Amendment 148 asks whether, for sexual and reproductive health informatio

hansard.debate: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (Subscription Contracts) (Consequential Amendments) Regulations 2026
hansard.speaker: Lord Clement-Jones (LD)
hansard.text: My Lords, I thank the Minister for introducing these two sets of regulations. I want to be clear from the outset that we on these Benches support the objective of Part 4, Chapter 2 of the DMCCA. We did so throughout its passage, and we support it now. Subscription traps are real: the free trial that quietly converts into a full-price commitment, the cancellation journey designed as an obstacle course and the annual renewal that arrives without warning. These practices cost consumers a considerable amount of money. I noticed that the Minister stated that these measures will save consumers some £436 million a year. Consumers deserve protection, and I believe that these regulations could provide much of it. However, the test of these regulations is not whether they are tough on the bad actors—I think they are—but whether they are workable and fair for the great majority of businesses, charities and publishers that do not set traps and whose subscribers, by the Government's own impact assessment, overwhelmingly want the subscriptions that they have. When we debated the primary legislation clauses in Grand Committee in February 2024, I described them as a blunt instrument and said they were both too vague and too detailed. I argued that much of the detail should be settled in secondary legislation after proper consultation and that it should come back to the House under an enhanced procedure to be properly scrutinised. That is broadly what has happened, and I welcome it. What I did not anticipate was the timetable: Royal Assent was in May 2024; the consultation ran from November 2024 to February 2025; and the Government's response came in April this year and pointed to implementation in spring 2027. These instruments were laid on 19 October and are due to come into force on

hansard.debate: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (Subscription Contracts) (Consequential Amendments) Regulations 2026
hansard.speaker: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (Lord Leong) (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, in moving the Motion on the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (Subscription Contracts) (Consequential Amendments) Regulations 2026, I will also speak to the Consumer Subscription Contracts (Cancellation and Information) Regulations 2026. These instruments implement the new consumer protections for subscription contracts that were set out in the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, known as the DMCCA. There are around 155 million active subscriptions in the United Kingdom, and consumers spend an estimated £2.1 billion a year on ones that they do not actually want. Subscriptions create ongoing financial liabilities and should therefore be a choice, not a trap. This legislation will place more control in the hands of the consumer to end ongoing contracts that they no longer value. Too often, someone thinks that they are making a one-off purchase only to find out months later that they have entered into a subscription. I am sure that many here—including me—have had the frustrating experience of trying to exit a contract only to find themselves lost in a laborious process and being forced to cancel by phone. The DMCCA introduces four measures: clear information before sign-up; regular reminders; straightforward exit processes; and cancellation rights, including during cooling-off periods. We anticipate that these measures will provide £436 million of consumer benefit per year. This means that each UK household will save around £15 per year, supporting the Prime Minister's commitment to giving people more breathing space from rising costs. hansard.debate: RFA Sir Galahad Board of Inquiry: Records Management and Disclosure
hansard.speaker: Louise Sandher-Jones
hansard.text: It is a bit unfair to say that we are hiding behind data protection. Again, I just would like to restate that I do not stand here with anything to hide. It is not my reputation that some people are trying to obscure in any way, shape or form. I was born long after the Falklands war started. There is absolutely no reason why I or my colleagues would try and conceal anything. What we try and respect is that there are legal rights and obligations. In this country, some people, in some circumstances, have a right to privacy as set out in law. I cannot just throw that away on the hoof. We must have due concern for that and be very careful about it. There is another point as well. Again, I do not say this as an absolute, but when it comes to service inquiries, I would like to assure those Members who raised it that the process has been considerably improved since the events of the Falklands war, although I am sure that there are always ways that it can still be improved. However, it is important that people feel that they can speak candidly and that the expectation is that their evidence will not be released in such a way as to prejudice them from being honest. It is important that we consider very carefully whether the wider impact of releasing reports to do with a historical event means that, in some future tragedy, we constrain being able to get to the truth. I appreciate that there is a judgment here. I am not saying that this is an absolute and I am not trying to hide behind it at all; I have a genuine and authentic concern that we must think of future boards of inquiry or investigations as well.

hansard.speaker: Baroness Monckton of Dallington Forest (Con)
hansard.text: My Lords, before I speak to Amendment 279QL standing in my name, I thank the noble Lord, Lord Scriven. I wholeheartedly support both his amendments. Mine is a probing amendment seeking a review of the challenges faced by people with speech, hearing and learning disabilities in accessing NHS care. We often speak in this House about waiting times and access to treatment, but access to healthcare begins with actually having the ability to book an appointment, describe symptoms, understand information and communicate effectively with a healthcare professional. That communication must be both ways. The healthcare professional needs to be able to communicate with this particular group. I have spoken before in this House about the drastic shortage across the country of learning disability nurses. This year, only 490 students enrolled in the learning disability nursing course, a 40% drop in the last decade. To put that into context, 4,768 learning disability nurses work for the NHS and there are 1.4 million people with a learning disability in this country. As a result of these falling numbers, people with learning disabilities are not being provided with their legal right to equitable care and access to health and care services. We all know that deaf people can struggle with telephone-based appointment systems, that people with speech and language difficulties can find it impossible to explain symptoms and that people with learning disabilities may not always receive the information in a manner that they can understand or even process. At its most serious, ineffective communication can become a patient safety issue, affecting a person's ability t

hansard.speaker: Lord Collins of Highbury (Lab)
hansard.text: The main point is that all systems have risks, not least the current one, which has many remote locations and is sometimes difficult to assess. We are striving to be more efficient. hansard.speaker: Lord Clement-Jones (LD)
hansard.text: My Lords, at the request of the noble Baronesses, Lady Noakes and Lady Freeman of Steventon, neither of whom can be in their places this morning due to parliamentary committee and outside commitments, I will respond to the Minister, particularly on Amendment 130. hansard.speaker: Baroness Harding of Winscombe (Con)
hansard.text: My Lords, I will speak to my Amendments 137A and 137B. I thank my noble friend Lady Shawcross-Wolfson—who not only added her name to them but did most of the drafting—and the noble Lords, Lord Tarassenko and Lord Patel, who added their names as well. I am a big supporter of the concept of a single patient record. I saw at first hand what was possible during Covid, when we were genuinely able to join up all the data. There is much talk about how our NHS data is a great national competitive strength. The reality is that it is not, unless we actually join up the data. Except in extreme emergencies, we are not able to do that. We do not really have a whole-population longitudinal health dataset for our life sciences to use to identify new treatments and to improve both patient outcomes and our economic growth. It is just an illusion without a proper single-patient record, so I am a huge supporter. But—and this is a big but—we need to recognise quite how scary it is to so many people to create a single patient record. Just the words are scary. Previous attempts to join up NHS data have not worked, not because of the technology but because we have not built and maintained patient and citizen trust. Trust is really hard to build and very easily broken. Unfortunately, in this space, it has been broken multiple times, whether we are talking about care.data, NPfIT or the federated data platform—I could keep going. In each case, we have failed to build citizen trust in our potential single datasets. I promise I will be brief. hansard.speaker: Lord Scriven (LD)
hansard.text: My Lords, I wish to speak as somebody who has worked in a commissioning organisation of the NHS, to explain that sometimes blunt data can be counterproductive when you are dealing with individuals, how they see themselves and how they wish their data to be used. We need to do something very important, which is to look at what already happens. The core information standards are the bible of how data is collected, recorded and used to ensure that services are provided in a way that meets not just individual need but the needs of particular disadvantaged communities. We have to be very careful about moving away from the principle that experts and people of a certain identity come together to work out what is in the best interest, collecting that data, using it, and then providing health services for individuals and groups of individuals based on that data. My noble friend Lady Barker is absolutely correct. The core information standard, version 2.01, now makes it mandatory to ensure that a person's biological sex at birth is on the individual record of every patient in the NHS. That is the stated aim. To put in the Bill that it also has to be on the single patient record misunderstands how the single patient record works. A single patient record is a conglomerate of individual care records and what has happened, so by default that will happen.

hansard.speaker: Lord Scriven (LD)
hansard.text: My Lords, I will speak quickly in this debate but not generally about the single patient record—my noble friend Lord Clement-Jones did that admirably. In contracting and design, are issues for people with learning disabilities and others who will need reasonable adjustments being built in by design and in contractual arrangements?

hansard.speaker: Lord Kakkar (CB)
hansard.text: My Lords, I support Amendments 133 and 143A, in the name of my noble friend Lord Patel, to which I have added my name. Fundamentally, his amendments address the real tension that your Lordships' House faces in considering Clause 52. On the one hand, there has been very strong support across the House for the principle of a single patient record, which will be a very powerful tool. We have heard how it will impact on improving clinical outcomes, driving patient safety and ensuring that valuable resources can be effectively applied where they are needed in the correct clinical care environment at the correct time. The single patient record is fundamental to the practice of modern medicine. It would be completely inappropriate, given that on repeated occasions your Lordships' House has agreed that there must be a transition from hospital community care, and where care environments will now be dispersed, if those providing that continuity of care, and indeed acute care, are unable to access core and key clinical information in real time for the benefit of their patient. On the other hand, we have seen on repeated occasions in the past 20 years attempts to apply or to address that important commitment to providing continuity of patient data undermined because the proposed approach has failed to secure an appropriate social licence. We have not secured broad consent on and confidence in the way the state would deal with the collective and deeply sensitive nature of those data and make them broadly available and easily accessible. That is the fundamental question that needs to be addressed in looking at Clause 52 and the introduction of new Section 250E into the NHS Act 2006, which is the purpose of the clause.

hansard.speaker: Lord Evans of Rainow (Con)

How will patients remain in control of their own data? How will they stay empowered to decide what they do and do not wish to be shared? How will the most sensitive information about them be accessed and by whom? The noble Lord, Lord Tarassenko, gave a graphic example on Monday night when he told the Committee about a patient going from one hospital to another. The hospital that the patient left gave over paper copies of the record and, on receipt of those, the receiving hospital digitised them, loading them on to the system. I remember that from Monday night; it was a good example of the issue that we have with some NHS hospitals. First, I will cover the concerns of the noble Lord, Lord Patel. When it is rolled out, the success of the SPR will rest on one thing above all: trust. If large numbers of patients do not trust either the system or their doctor, we will face mass patient opt-outs. If the medical profession decides that it does not trust the system, doctors will cease to co-operate with it. Either or both these eventualities would strangle the system at birth. We cannot afford to let that happen. The duty of medical confidentiality is, for doctors, sacrosanct: it underpins the doctor-patient relationship. In creating the holy grail of the single patient record, we cannot simply shrug off an expediency-led breach of that duty, which would be inherent in the process of uploading data on to the SPR platform. The fact that an overriding public interest justification may permit a departure from the common-law duty will not get round how patients ultimately feel about someone other than the doct

hansard.speaker: Baroness Shawcross-Wolfson (Con)

I am hugely supportive of public interest research. Clearly, there are incredible opportunities here to further our scientific understanding and ultimately improve outcomes for patients but, as I argued in the debate on the previous group of amendments about the SPR, patients will need to understand how the development of a single patient record, the reform of the COPI regulations and the Health Data Research Service all fit together. They may be three different programmes in the department, but they cannot be considered in silos because of the combined effect. I think we all agreed in our previous debate that trust in the SPR depends on patients having clarity on how their data could be used, including for secondary research.

hansard.text: My Lords, it is a pleasure to follow the noble Baroness, Lady Harding, and her discussion of the importance of trust. I am grateful to noble Lords who added their names to my Amendment 162, which is about the need to protect confidential psychological therapy records. I speak as a now retired psychiatrist and psychotherapist, and argue that detailed psychotherapy session narratives should be excluded from routine sharing by default. This should not mean that the whole record is then not shared; it is still essential that information about medication, allergies, risk to self or others, crisis plans and other information necessary for safe care remain available. In psychotherapy, confidentiality affects treatment itself. Patients need to be able to disclose difficult material—for example, feelings of anger and hate—and to trust that it will be held securely. I would particularly value the Minister's consideration of whether the clinical consequences of routine narrative sharing have been assessed. A patient whom the Guardian calls “Rosanna” asked me to share her experience. I note that the noble Lord, Lord Clement-Jones, spoke briefly about her challenge to the London Care Record on Monday evening. We should learn what we can from this case. To clarify, for the noble Lord, Lord Evans, and others, this is not about removing patient-clinician confidentiality. It is important that we retain trust, which is why I make that point particularly. This is about making sure that doctors are not inhibited from sharing information in a secure and confidential system because they may have concerns that they are

hansard.text: My Lords, I thank all noble Lords who have spoken on this group, and the Government for the clear way in which the amendments were introduced. Taxpayers are entitled to expect proper accountability for how their money spent. Equally, Parliament should have sufficie

hansard.speaker: Baroness Finlay of Llandaff (CB)
hansard.text: My Lords, I am very grateful to the noble Lord, Lord Hunt of Kings Heath, for tabling these amendments; I added my name to Amendment 207. I must declare that I am patron of the Commonwealth Tribute to Life, which was set up through NHS Blood and Transplant to promote ethical transplantation. It is a voluntary network for Commonwealth health ministries, transplant services and clinicians to share practice without charge or conditions. We have a network right across the Commonwealth, with much of the Commonwealth covered. But it is seven years since the Organ Donation (Deemed Consent) Act was passed, and it is time to review our current system of organ donation because it is not working as it should for families and patients. hansard.speaker: Lord Leong (Lab)
hansard.text: My Lords, I am grateful for the contributions from all noble Lords on these two instruments. Let me start by addressing the point about businesses, perishable goods, cancellation and so on. The way I look at it is that businesses should be confident of their own business and what they produce and supply. They should also recognise that, whatever they produce or supply, some people may not want it, so there is a possibility of returns or even cancellation. I remember from when I was a publisher—I am sure that the noble Lords here who are authors will know this—that publishers supply their books to booksellers on a sale-or-return basis. We move our books from our warehouse to a bookshop, which puts the books on the shelf. If the books do not sell, the shop returns them to the publisher three months later. More often than not, 80% of the books are not resaleable, so we publishers have to raise a credit note against the invoice of the books supplied and pulp the books that are not resaleable. That is part of our cost of doing business. Likewise, if I am a perishable goods supplier, I will supply my goods and have to recognise the fact that, after trying them, the customer may not like what I supply. They have every right to return them or to cancel their subscription. If the goods are on their way, the business has to look at its business model and say, “This is part of the cost of doing business”. That is how businesses operate. The cost is always there in that some goods will be returned.

They served our country with pride and dignity and were an example to us all, and it is a stain on this Government that we allowed that to happen. It is often said that a lie will go around the world before the truth has its boots on, and that is what the Welsh Guards faced.
